THE CHURCH SOCIETY.
Ask For Careful Preparations For National Mission.

The Rev. Canon Willis (rector) presided at the annual meeting of the Warrington Churl, Society, held on Monday in the Church House, others present being: Rev. G. Vale Owen (hon. sec.),' Mr. C. A. Littler (hon. treasurer), Canon Stevenson, Rev. J. Davies, Messrs. F. Pearson, J. H. Smethurst, W. Milner, W. H. Stansfield, Miss M. 'Reynolds and Mrs. Guest Gornall. The resignation of Mr. John Hesketh, a member of the committee, was received with much regret, especially as the cause was owing to ill-health. A resolution was passed record- ing his services to the society from its forma- tion. _ _ _

The twenty-fourth annual report, which was adopted by the meeting and presented by the Rev. G. Vale Owen, expressed the committee's thanks to the preachers and lecturers who had kindly helped during the past year. The com- mittee reminded members of the National Mission of Repentance and Hope to be held from Sunday, October 22nd, to Sunday, Octob.n. 29th, and urged them to rendet all help pos- sible in the preparation for the same. Attention was drawn to the preparation services held on the last Saturday ,of each month ,at 4 p.m. Two of these services had already been held, and others would take place as follows:—June 24th, St. Barnabas'; July 29th, St. Ann's; August 26th, Holy Trinity; September 30th, St. Peter's.

div.head: "WAR MANDATE."
div.p: "WAR MANDATE."
Should There Be An Immediate Election ?

In pursuance of a campaign for the speedy, rigorous and effectual prosecution of the war to a definite issue by means of a new Parliament in England, Dr. Arthur Turnbull addressed an open-air meeting in Warrington last Saturday. He re- marked that this view for a new Parliament, based on a direct war mandate, was for the sup- port of the Government and the Army, and had already been stated at Sunderland, Newcastle, Hull, Derby, Nottingham, Leicester, and other towns in the North of England. The reasons were mainly three :- 1. The election of a new House would drive home the realisation of the truth to the Ger- mans, namely, that they were confronted not merely by the English Government, or by the English Army, but also by the English people. That realisation of our national unity and de- termination will assuredly shorten the war. The English people alone in Europe have the right of free government by the orderly procedure of their Parliamentary institutions, and if they choose not to exercise that right they are assuming a heavy responsibility for the furtherd and definite setting of high explosives against flesh and blood. Only English justice, law and order could conquer German force. _ .
2. A new Parliament should be there ready to state an explicit business agreement to the representatives of the German people, whenever that people were in a fit and humble mood to receive them. _ .

_ 3. Pending the acceptance of a just and im- partial contract 'by them, England must fight. A stern and swift fight was not possible on our present lines. It could come only by ap- pointing a war directorate, so that each €hief of each section of the war business would be in sole and undividedly responsible charge of his particular section. These sections were: Navy. Army, air, home defence, Munitions, dtstructive science, recruiting, food, transport, engineering, Press, finance (Government contracts), blockade. These men to be guided by a director-in-chief, who, like the other 13, should be unpaid and responsible to the Houk) of Commons. The method of election recommended was a rapid election upon one single and appointed day. The voters to be those bearing the cost of war in blood and money, namely, every man and woman in England, Scotland and Wales, of the age of 21 years and upwards. Only England could bring order' and freedom for ',the chaos of destruction, disease and death, which obtained to-day through Eur9Pe• Let England iact.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 24, 1916.

As the pre-war dinner gown is-no longer a necessity, and indeed is seldom seen, the afternoon gown, and demi- toilette have greatly increased in importance; they have also become much more unsubstan- tial, and are now made of the filmiest materials. Summer-time also has altered the diurnal con- ditiOns of the dinner' hour, and a dress that suited artificial light perfectly, seems out of place by daylight. The Empress Eugenie.

The Queen and Princess Mary went recently to Farnborough to see the aged ex-Empress of the French, who lately celebrated her ninetieth birthday. The Empress is still in the enjoy- ment of fairly good health, and of all her .fadul- ties, despite her many sorrows and trials. div.head: LORD FRENCH'S GREAT IDEA.
div.p: LORD FRENCH'S GREAT IDEA.
The Mantle Of Voluntaryism.

Two incidents of supreme. importance to this country have taken place within the last few days. Small in themselves, when com- pared with ,the stupendous happenings we are witnessing from day to day, these inci- dents have a bearing that for Englishmen goes to the very heart of things. During the week an Army Order has been issued declaring that bodies of men may again bp enrolled under the Volunteer Act of 1863, ana the KING has been pleased to accept the offer of certain persons desiring to be formed into Volunteer Corps. We notice that in the schedule accompanying this Order eleven Corps in Cheshire are to be enrolled., The schedule, does not 'contain any from Lancashire, but that defect may, be remedied by those further offers • which, we 'are informed, may be submitted to His MAJESTY. This Order follows upon. the notable speech made by LORD FRENCH last Saturday, when he reviewed 10,000 London Volunteers, and announced, plainly and Un- equivocally, that the KING highly appreciated the devoted loyalty the Volunteers have shown since the outbreak of the war, and that the War Office also highly appreciated their services.

• An idea was very prevalent that the War Office did not want the Volunteers, and that they were disposed to look upon them as a possible means of checking the stern work which the needs of the Army demanded at the moment. LORD FRENCH dissipated that idea at once, and asked the Volunteers to turn it out pf, their minds completely. As a man who led our great Army in France and Bel- gium for a long and most important period of the war, and speaking now as head of the Home Defence, he described the Volunteers he had seen since his return to England as "bodies of smart-looking men, of very sol- dierly appearance, full of earnestness, march- ing and drilling." The Commander-in-Chief, if he did not apologise for past neglect, at least explained why apparent neglect had taken place. You cannot call a man a soldier, in this country, by putting a gun into his hand, he said; departments have to be con- sulted and Parliament has to have its say. But well that ends well, and now that the time that is necessary to allow the Eng- lish mind to get to work haskelapsed, the Vol- unteers are to, be accepted and welcomed into the defensive forces of the country. But the main point of LORD FRENCH'S re- marks lay in the reminder that the Volun- teers represent a grand .idea. In the early part of the second half of last century the Volunteers fought hard to force their patriotic services upon a somewhat indifferent country. They succeeded, and when the day of trial came they proved that their ardour had been right and the coolness of the , country had been t wrong. Let Its imagine, if ive can, where we would have been, in whose hands Paris would have been, had not the Terri- torials been ready to guard thg country against invasion while our Expeditionary Force threw itself in the path of the oncoming Germans at Mons. We have lately adopted compulsion, temporarily, and the Volunteers have become the standard-bearers for volun- taryitm in England to see ifs over a most try- ing period in its history. It is to LORD FRENCH'S mind a great idea to regard these Corps as the people upon whom the mantle of the 'Volunteers, who are buildingup "a glorious record "in France, has fallen. It should surely not neecl, the threats of the Military Tribunals to get' recruits, for these Corps, who are maintaining an ideal that goes to the root of British liberty. All men who are not actually serving with the Colours are invited to enrol themselves as Volunteers. At War- rington, Grappenhall, Stockton Heath, Lymm ' and Other centres, Corps are in being, and the officials of each of them will be delighted to direct any man as to the best methods to adopt to do his duty to his country in its present need.

div.head: CALL TO ACTION.
div.p: CALL TO ACTION.
Rev. T. T. James And The Church's Responsibility.
NEED FOR STRENGTH.
The Rev. T. T. James - began his series of six sermons at Wycliffe Church on •" The Church -and the War," last Sunday evening, when he spoke on "Church Worship and the Time of Crisis."

The present, he said, was a critical time for all \ organisations and institutions; it was pre- eminently so for the Church. Others might content themselves by tiding over these days to await the opportunities of better times, but for the Church of Christ the vital question was, What part is she playing in the hour of our greatest need? In times of crisis the things that mattered were separated from the thingi that had no value: the present was the hour 'Ahen the Church was to be tested by its fitness to meet the facts of the existing situa- tion. It would stand or fall by the power it showed to deal with that unique situation. These days of crisis presented themselves to Christian men and women as an unexampled opportunity. Granted that war was a method of settling disputes which ages of progress should have taught us to outgrow, was it not worth while to remember how the great calamity had emphasised our spiritual need?
IS BLOOD AND MUD ORGY TO BE THE LAST WORD ?

"It seems," said the reverend gentleman, "such a simple thing by pow fora 'lad to don the King's uniform that \we are :inclined to forget to • how many millions it has meant facing the fact whether duty was to be con- sidered more than life itself. I am not saying that every lad who enrolled his name went through a stern struggle in which he con- fronted, the possibility that hit.; action might mean the surrender of his life, but I am say- ing that very many did so, and that even the wildest and most exuberant spirit, - knowing nothing of fear and keen for agventure, mast have given stnne passing glance to the fat* that he took and must take his life in his 'hand. And for. those whose place is here at home, have any circumstances eirer arisen in our day before, sci" 'eloquent to us of the chance and change of mere material things, the -slender certainty of this world's pomp and splendour and power? And do we' imagine that ever before more men and women were eiimpelled to face the ultimate questions, men and women compelled' to them by the facts of personal anxiety or personal tragedy? "And this orgy of mud ~and blood, is this to be the last word inc the world about our idealism, is this the last glory which is ,to oc painted for men to aim at, the last thing be held up before their eyes two thousand years after Christ died upon the Cross, or is there some message still to speak of a nobler day when in the brotherhood of the race mercy and truth shall. Meet together and righteousness and peace shall kiss each other?" Stirely it is true that with these •ultimate question S forced upon us, something of our pre- occupation with the superficial and secondary things of life ,ha passed away, and as never before the spiritual needs of men have been made clear to our gaze. This is what I mean by saying that this day, howel'er we may con- ceive it as difficult and heavy, must also be conceived as an unexampled opportunity for the Church of Christ.

div.head: GRAVE CONFESSION.
div.p: A GRAVE CONFESSION.

This ,situation would be met only by a living Church. It took a living Church to deal with the actual facts of life; and the first sign of ja living Church was the realrty of its worship. The Church, was .a bgdy of men sand women organised for worship, and where it was not serving that purpose it was missing the most vital of all its activities. That worship niast be a collective and co-operative 'spiritual effort on the part of all concerned. • "It has to be confessed," he continued, "that not even the world tragedy ofi these days has succeeded iij restoring thecdt4rict between vast masses of the nation :and the Church of Jesus Christ, and it is a ,confession which ,must be made with the gravest concern: It ig far too large a question to be discussed in a sentence or two, but there is one simple line of action which is immediately open to Christian men and women. Those who belong to the Church can make up their minds that by their own loyalty and devotion to its work and worship they will give .a witness to the value they place upon it. The first step towards convincing •those outside the Church that there is some- thing within of worth and value will come from the. strengthening of the inward life of the Church. We shall not persuade the world out- side to put a greater , value on the 'Church and what it offers than we put on it ourselves. The first and fore- most task of the Church is to make its worship a living thing, for apart from that it will not make and shake by its #afluence living men and women." ,

"When, English homes are flooding foreign lands with unnamed graves," the preacher. con- cluded, "when the sight of a telegram is making the heart stand still in your home or the one next to it, when empires are shaking and tot- tering and history is being made by leaps and 'bounds, we are back in the elemental things again: it is the very atmosplrre in which we live. Oh, my brothers, I do not know whether even God Himself will ever be /able to make anything of., the man who does not hear His voice to-day. I do not know whether the Church that cannot worship amidst this tragedy of- human need will ever be able to worship: reality for it must. be dead. I do lot know ,whether . the ,nation in wham thi.: does not arouse _the demand for a religious faith has any future whether it win the war or not. "This is a great day for the Church and for the people of God. It is an unexampled opportunity. Only it is a tremendous responsi- bility, the like of which We have not known before. We peed the strength and will to welcome it. We need the grace to deal with it. And it ought to be on all our minds until we say not with any formality, but with all the passion of our hearts: 'We will take care of che Church of God.'"

Difference Between Elementary Education Of Past & Present.
TRAINING COLLEGE PRINCIPAL AND THE CRITICS.

When submitting his report at the prize dis- tribution at the Warrington Training College on Saturday afternoon, the Principal (the Rev. Canon Stevenson) replied to critiPs of our elementary school education, and 489 made some suggestions where there might"Ye" an im- provement. "We are told that the war will bring about great changes in education," he said. "A good deal has been written in the newspapers in reference to the present system, which we are assured is rotten from top to bottom, and most of all is that alleged in the case of elementary schools. They say that there should be drastic changes, and the whole system of education is to be revolutionised. I take some comfort 'to myself under this douche of criticism because I am able to go back mtny years with as 'inti- mate a knowledge of education and of elementary schools as probably most people have, and all I can say is that the elementary school of to-day as compared with the elementary school of 50 years ago is as wine to water. I don't know your sentiments. You might like to say as water to wine—(laugh- ter)—but the existing elementary school is com- parably, as far as I can see, a better thing. I can remember the bad days in which schools were judged by the percentage of passes in each subject, when the livelihood of teachers de- pended more or less upon those passes, when children were over-pressed and over-driven and teachers were worried and anxious, and the whole school life of the child instead of being a life of happiness was in many cases a life ot misery. When, therefore, I look upon the school of the present day I don't fear very much for 'the criticism which is coming, and I take heart also for another reason. We are always being told that the curriculum of our schools is all wrong. It has always been all wrong according to the critic. (Laughter.) If I may venture to express an opinion I should say that there is very little wrong with the curriculum at the present moment, and that teaching and the Sub- jects taught are eminently fitted for the best intellectual atmosphere of the children. I should, however, like to see the school life of the children lengthendd, the classes of a more reasonable size; and with one or two reforms of this kind parried out we shall have taken a long step towards the betterment of education than by any amount of tinkering with the curriculum in use." (Hear, hear, and applause.) Proceeding, the Principal emphasised the fact that in that college they had adopted the polipy of making the training of the teacher The great and foremost object, and academic success a secondary one. More time was given to the training of teachers to practical work in schools, because the object of a training college should be to turn out good teachers. He was thankful to say that that college stood high in reputation in this part of England for the ex- cellende of the teaching which its ex-students gave in the schools. He heard that on all sides, and the fact' was proved by the astonishing number of ,headships held in the neighbour- hood of Warrington by Warrington girls. (Ap- plause.) div.p: AN ARTISTIC MINISTER.
Spendthrift In Pictures, But Not In Clothes.
REV. JOS. HOWARD DIES IN ARMCHAIR.

While sitting in his arm-chair treading a newspaper after breakfast on Thursday last week, there passed away at his residence, Sankey 'Hall, Great Sankey, an extraordinary Wesleyan supernumerary minister in the per- son of the Rev. Joseph Howard. He was in)his eightieth year. Well-to-do (his large investments in Canada had yielded ten-fold) he spent a great deal on pictures and hardly anything on clothes. Caring the-least of all men for personal appear- ances, he will be recollected by the general public who saw him only in the streets, as a healthy-faced minister of religion who looked as sturdy as a geptleman farmer, and walked briskly in elderly boots and an age-worn frock coat. He was never without his old-fashioned satchel He was always by himself, for he had few friends, and was regarded as a recluse. His interest in art amounted to a passion. There is scarcely a picture dealer in the country who did not have transactions with him, for, especially in the years of his retire- ment from circuit work about sixteen years ago, he was continually ,touring the country in search of art treasures. Consequence: the whole of' the rooms at Sankey Hill are lined with valuable paintings. In some rooms you cannot see wallpaper for pictures. He specialised in old paintings, and many of those which now look the brightest he brought home in a soiled condition, cleaning them with the scrupulous and fastidious care of the artist.

In many other ways the reverend gentleman displayed unconventionality. No woman ever entered his home to do housework, he and one of his sons, who does not enjoy the best -3f health, doing this between them, the old gentleman manifesting much of the vigour and adaptability of a soldier in barracks.
A Difference With The Corporation.

In matters of business the reverend gentla- I man always 'sought to make a good bargain. I The Warrington Corporation had evidence bf I that in preparing their scheme for the circus lat Market Gate. For the success of this it was lessential that the house and shop, No. 7, Buttermarket-street, in which Ithe reverend gentleman had a life inteiest, should be pulled down. On being approached Mr. Howard, on the advice of his valuer, demanded £2,340, with the result that arbitration proceedings were held, the Corporation's valuer stating that £955 was a fair and proper sum, and the valuer to the Assessment Committee fixing the amount at an even lower figure-025. The arbitrators allowed £1,245, or just over half of 'what he asked for, and about 000 more thzin he was offered. Mr. Howard' was owner of' extensive land in Canada, two of his sons at one time wbrking one of the farms there. He paid them three visits and, being an acute observer and :n- -..teresting talker, he entertained his friends ,on his return - with excellent stories of what he saw out West. Whenever he spoke from' a Unionist platform in the Newton Division (he, was an ardent supporter.of Lord Wolmer) his mind always drifted away to Canada, and be could not avoid expatiating of the 'wonderful possibilities and development of our Empire. Born at Latchford, the son of the late Mr. Thomas Howard, of Sankey Hall Farm. the reverend gentleman early showed expository faculties, and while being educated at Owen's College he devoted his Sundays to local preaching, revealing special aptitude for euen- air work. He was very successful at' College, and was not called upon to undergo the special training usually given before being , accepted into the Wesleyan ministry. For over, forty years he ably served his dehi.minatiln as a circuit minister in various parts of the country. his sermons 'were always charac- terised by earnestness and thoughtfulness, and he had a wonderful commanl of words which often led /him to continue his discourses well over an hour.

div.p: Interested in the Established Church.

A Wesleyan minister of a strictly orthodox type as far as doctrine dictated, he was yet intensely interested in the Established ,Church, and frequently attended Grappenhall /Church. He could trace his ancestors in that village back to the fourteenth century as tenants of the Merburys and other landowners, and it was his desire at one time to have erected in che church a stained glass window to honour their memory. Faculty had been granted for this Purpose, and then war broke out, with he result that Mr. Howard told his friend the Vicar (the Rev. H. V. Pigot) that the scheme had better lie over until peace was declared. On his retirement he took up his residence with his Sister at Stockton Heath, but after a short timp he bought Sankey Halt, situated in a, district which had for him hallowed memories. Well within his view stood the house where he was born. Until three years ago, when a motor cycle. knocked him down just, outside his home, the reverend gentleman frequently occupied pulpits in' the Warrington circuit, but latterly he had not felt equal to the task of preaching. His death, however, came with suddenness.

It may be added that the 60 per year which was sent to hini from the Fund for Worn-out Wesleyan Ministers was always returned with an expression of thanks And a declaration that he was able to do without it, and hoping that it would be divided among others whose finances were at a low ebb.

div.head: LICENSEE AS FARMHAND.
div.p: LICENSEE AS FARMHAND.
Works In Field During The Day And In Bar At Night.

At the Warrington Rural District Tribunal on Thursday conditional exemption was given to a Burtonwood licensee, who works on various farms during the day and in his bar at night. It was stated that every morning he milks twenty-two cows.—Mr. T. S. Steel appeared on his' behalf, and emphasised the fac-Fthat the applicant is an experienced thatcher and hay- cutter, as well as milk Man. • Another licensee—this time from Fearnhead— applied for exemption. The military represen- tative (Mr. W. Furness) explained that the ap- plicant had appealed before and been refused. For eighteen months, in additibil to being a licensee, he had worked for his brother, who owned a small factory, engaged on making munitions. It was now suggested that as the applicant was technically very skilled, and an- other man had just left the works, the licensee should be allowed to remain.—The Tribunal agreed to conditional exemption being given. "This is a good man. I paid £9 to get him here from Yorkshire, and should not like to lose him," said Walter ,Bennett. of Bruche Farm, Padgate, in applying for his cownaal—Condi- tional exemption was granted.

div.head: " Unstarred," But Exempted.
div.p: " Unstarred," But Exempted.

By reason of the new regulation p a young man who had been exempted was now automatically " unstarred " owing to his youth, but his em- ployer, J. L. Fryer, .a farmer, of Padgate, made a strong appeal for him, emphasising that he was the only man of military age on the farm.— Conditional exemption. Two farming brothers at Martinscroft were conditionally exempted, and another brother, aged 22 years, was given until the 30th Septem- ber. Another brother, aged 20 years, is at the Front. The one who has been temporarily ex- empted had expressed his willingness to join the Army after the date mentioned. The farm ex- tends to forty acres. All His Savings.

A Sankey man, who gave up wiredrawing in order to become a milkman, because of his health, was conditionally exempted, Mr. T. S. Steel Appearing on his behalf. All his savings have been put into the business. His wife is in too poor health to carry if on. James Gandy, farmer, of Fearnhead, appealed for his teamsman, married, and aged 36 years, and was given exemption until the 30th Septem- ber. The farm is of 48 acres. The farmerl suffers from bronchial catarrh and has to go to bed two months every year. At other times he is unable to do much hard work. His father, aged 63 years, is unableqo work a great deal. Besides the man appealed for and those mentioned, there is only a man aged 70 years on the farm. A Padgate .man, aged 37, .carrying on busiiteas as a fruiterer and potato dealer, told the Tri- bunal that he had four children dependent and a mother partially dependent upon him. He had no one to carry on the business if he left.— Two months was allowed in which to arrange his business affairs.

The Runcorn Rural District Local Tribunal sat on Thursday and disposed of an extremely long list, there being ninety-eight applications for either temporary or total exemption. WORK ON FARMS.

div.head: What Would Happen If You Say Much
div.p: What Would Happen If You Say Much
To -Women.

The majority of the applications were put for- ward on behalf of men employed in farm work, either as cowmen, horsemen, or teamsmen. The Clerk pointed out a section in the regulations which suggested that where a man contributed materially to the food supply, and it was clear that no substitute could be found, he should be generally retained in civil employment. In the greater number of cases the Tribunal granted conditional exemption, and the reliainder, with one or two exceptions, were exempted to the Ist Octfiber. Most of the farmers applying on be- half of 'employes were asked why they could not engage women, but there was evidently a con- sensus of opinion against female" labpdr. Mr. Antwis (a member of the Tribunal) remarked: "They would run you out of the place if you say much to them." (Laughter.) In all cases where exemptions were granted the Tribunal made it a condition that the men should join their local Volunteer Training Corps, and put in as much time in drilling as possible. The Refuge Assurance Company applied for exemption on behalf of their divisional inspec- tor, aged 40, who has charge of the district hay. jug Warrington as its centre. The details of the business done by the company were given by Mr. Swift, head official in the chief office, who further mentioned that some sixty per cent. of their men had gone up for enlistment. A la - etition in support of thp appeal was handed in, the document 'being signed by eight medical men in the Stockton Heath dis- trict, who jpintly testified to the invaluable ser- vices which this man rendered to them and the public generally by keeping their cars in repair. —Conditional exemption was granted. div.head: Making Very Rapid Progress
div.p: Making Very Rapid Progress
Towards Recovery.

Lieutenant-Colonel George Crosfield, D. 5.0., who last week was mentioned in dispatches for the third tithe during the course of the present war, is still staying with his brother, Sir Arthur Crosfield, Bart., at 41, West Hill, Highgate, London. Highgate, with its 'in- vigorating atmosphere and pleasant surround- ings, is combining with the gallant Colonel's physical powers and optimistic disposition in effecting a cure as complete as the circum- stances of the case will allow. At any rate, we understand the authorities at the London hospital he was in are astonished at the pip- gress he has been making. He now gets aboilt the grounds and gardens with a fair amount of comfort, and is in very good spirits.

div.head: TERRITORIALS.
div.p: TERRITORIALS.
Col. Fairclough's Thanks For Kindly Remembrancers.

The Town Clerk hasi received the following letter from Colonel Brereton Fairclough, officer commanding the Warrington Territorials:— " Dear Mr. Whittle,—The cases of cigarettes and tobacco have just come to hand and Are being distributed. Please thank the kind people who provide for the gift; they probably little realise how much their forethought is appreciated, mit only for most acceptable extra supply of cigarettes, but also for the moral assistance they are rendering. These gifts tell the men, that, although they are out of sight of home, they are far from being forgotten.

div.head: Fun For The Natives.
div.p: Fun For The Natives.

"About a week ago the Battalion had an afternoon at sports, and the various competi- tions, were very well entered for and the 'finishes were very close. The &lives turned I out gradually to see the fun, and towards the end there were a fair number present—they all seemed -to enjoy the comic events very much, especially tilting the bucket. All the spec- tators seemed thoroughly disappointed at one entry: two officers, the bucket Xpus four gallons of water) tilted beautifully, but they had got so much speed on that they got clear beifore the water had time to reach them. This entry was the Doctor wheeled by the Padre in a wheelbarrow. A regular disappointed howl of 'Oh' went round when they got clear. The prizes were distributed afterwards by the C.R.E., who made a short speech on the value of healthy competitions such as he had wit- nessed that afternoon, not only from a pleasure point 6f-view, but also from the training stand- point.

div.head: Cold And Rain.
div.p: Cold And Rain.

"We are having rather a chilly time of it at present, summer having set in with its usual sever*. Being more or less slaves of habit, we 'cast our clouts when May was out, but very soon put them on again. It does not actually freeze at night, but considering the time of the year, we think ,the weather i mak- ing a very gond try.

"I really must stop now and get warm some- how. I've been writing this sitting in my billet, three windows broken, one cracked and the door won't close properly, and I'm wearing a greatcoat. Lord, how it is raining! It looks like millions of fine strizigs of water being wound into the earth from the sky."

div.head: Mit. ROGER PARR.
div.p: Mit. ROGER PARR.
Working For The 'Wounded And Missing In France.

Mr. Roger C. Parr, honorary treasurer of the Warrington Infirmary, who is engaged in the inquiry .department for wounded. and missing of the British Red Cross Society and St. John Ambulance Association at a great hospital centre in France, writing to Mr. J. J. .Elampson, secretary of the Infirmary, says:— "I like the work better in London than, here: they inove the men on so quickly (often less than 24 hours) it is so impossible to see them, and then they are often so tired and sleepy they don't care much about being questioned. There are really miles of hospitals here, hotels, casinos, huts, tents some with 2,000 beds and more, all so beautifully managed. If you hear of anybody from Warrington I might see them. The authorities are very strict about letters, and giving leave to go from one place to another. There are five of us doing this work here, which is very interesting and very sad. As a convoy comes in daily or oftener it is most difficult to keep pace with the: men. It is so cold, too, and we have fires every night; quite unlike June. I saw Mr. Vincient Davies pass- ing through this last week; it was curious see- ing hipa here." -

HORSE DEALER'S SUCCESSFUL APPEAL TO COUNTY TRIBUNAL.

Before the County Appeal Tribunal sitting at Liverpool, on Tuesday, the Lord Mayor pre- siding, a horse dealer and forage merchant, carrying on business at Orford, appealed against the decision of the Warrington Rural District Tribunal, who had granted him ex- emption until the 16th August, which they had declared, to be final. Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for the appellant, who, it was stated, had , been married for 14 years and had two children. ' At the com- mencement. of the war he had five men work- ing ,for him and they had attended exclusively to horses, but they had since joined the Forces and he had been unable to replace them. He had supplied horses to Government buyers and also supplied horses to The largest firms of nianufa,cturers for 'some considerable distance around Warrington. He had spent a consider- able sum on his stables and house, which, if he were called up, he would lose. He did a considerable business in buying and e,ellihg all kinds of forage, for which purpose he had to travel long distances. His wife was in a deli- cate state of health' and was at present wider the care of a local medical man. If he were called up for service it was contended that great hardship would ensue, and particulars were given to the Tribunal to bear, out this, contention.
IThe Tribunal allowed the appeal and granted the appellant until the 30th September, with - liberty- to apply again.

he was with the firm of Campbell, Pithlado and Co., barristers, having in the meantime been for a short period in the office of Messrs. Rawle, Johneone and Co., Mr. Longton's London agents. He was married, eighteen months ago, to Miss Trixie Scott, of Sheffield, whom he met on the boat when going to Canada, four years ago. :(illed During the Canadian Countet--Attack, It was during the recent suocessful counter- ,ttack upon the Germans that Private Car- lisle met his death. A comrade, writing to 3lrs. If there is anything I can do for you at all in your trouble, please do not be afraid to call on me; shall only be too willing. Frank and I had a deep /attach- lnent, formed thtough many a little hardship, And you may be sure his death has been a sad loss to .me. With all sympathy from his corporal and platoon, myself and other com- rades."

div.head: PRIVATE J. CASWELL.
div.p: PRIVATE J. CASWELL.
Four Soldier-Brothers ; Two Killed.

Posted as missing since June 4th of last year, Private John Caswell, of the K.0.5.8.'5, a married man, of 3, Wright-street,-is now pre- sumed to have fallen in action on that date. News to that effect has reached his wife from the War Office. , Private Caswell was one of the four soldier sons of Mr. and Mrs. T. Caswell, 13, Percy. street, and the second to give his life in the country's cause. His younger brother, Samuel, was killed in action in July, 1915. Another brother, Walter, lost an eye while at the Front, while, another, *Thomas, is also on active service. Private John was formerly employed at Messrs. Locker's, wire manufac- turers, Ellesmere-street, and was also engaged as an emergency man at the Royal Court Theatre. He leaves four childten in additioik to a widow.

div.head: PRIVATE T. SMITH.
div.p: PRIVATE T. SMITH.
Official News As To The Fate Of Local Territorial.

An °Nal letter has reached• Mr. and Mrs. T. Smith, of 70, Forshaw-street, stating that as no further news has been received of their son, Private Thomas Smith, of the local Terri- torials, who was reported missing on 16th June, 1915, the authorities can only arrive at the conclusion that he met his death on or about that date.

A widower, 27 years of age, Private Smith lived with his parents before rejoining the Army in August, 1914. He had previously served for six, years. He was employed as a wiredrawer by the Whitecross Co., Ltd. He was educated at Heathside School, and attended Emmanuel Church.

div.head: CORPORAL ISHERWOOD.
div.p: CORPORAL ISHERWOOD.
Popular N.C.O. Who Has Been
Buried! At Cairo.

Mr. and Mrs. H. Isherwood, Heathfield, ?air.. field-road, Latchford Without, have this Week received details concerning the death at Caro of their eldest son, Corporal Frank Forster Isherwood, M.T. A.S.C. It appears he was taken ill on Tuesday, May 30th, and was ad- mitted into hospital, where an operation for appendicitis was carried out on the Thursday. He died at 1.30 on the Saturday morning. He was buried with full military honours ,at 5.30 in the afternoon in Old Cai,ro Cemetery. The
Died in Egypt

Rev. J. Baget de la Bare, chaplain to the Popes, officiated. About 150 officers, non-com- missioned ofiloers and men attended, six of his brother corporals acting as pall-bearers. At the close of the ceremony "The Last Post" was sounded by the buglers. Mr. and Mrs. Isherwood have received many letters of sympathy. - Major Maconochie-Wel- wood, the officer commanding his company, says Corporal 'lsherwood was very popular with everyone in the unit. He has lost in him "a straightforward, reliable and good N.C.0." Lieutenant McLaurin writes: "He v4as one of. the most popular and best-liked non--commis- sioned officers in the company and his promo- tion to the rank of sergeant was already assured, and would have taken place in a few days' time." Company-Sergeant-Major Rogeiw says: "We have lost oneiof our best men.- In the course of a week or so he would have been made eergeant. He was so well liked that I made him a member of the Sergeants' Mess." His fellow-corporals write that Ifherwood was "one of the best." .
Corporal Isherwood was engaged in the War- rington Water Engineer's office.
CORPORAL FRANK F. ISHERWOOD.

Eighteen motor curs and chars-a-bane carry- ing 108 happy, smiling children left Bold-street Wesleyan Church at about 1.30 p.m. on Thurs- day for Overton, near Frodsham. The occasion was the annual outing given by the Warring- ton Cripples' Guild to Warrington and district cripples, a fete to which the latter always look 'forward. Although the weather bon- ditions were none foo promising, the enthusi- asm'of the cripples was none the less, and,, as they commenced their journey, they were accorded a hearty send-off by a number of rela- tives and friends, amongst whom was his Worship the Mayor. The destination of the cripples was the National Children's Home and Orphanage at Overton, near Frodsham, and the route taken lay through Stockton Heath, Stretton, Whit- ley, Acton Bridge, Weaverham and Kingsley. The children sang merrily throughout the journey, and the massive trees, now in their pomp, which line the roads of these beautifpl country places, echoed and re-echoed with the notes of "Keep the home fires burning," "It's, a long wi4, to Tipperary," and "God Save th King," which came from the throats of more than a hundred boys and girls. Overton was reached about threi o'clock, and the cripples were accorded a hearty welcome by the inmates of the Children's Home. The visitors were soon partaking of a substantial tea, after which they could play in the groan is adjoining the home, or go for strolls in the beautiful surrounding country. ;Unfortun- ately rain fell for a time later on \in the after- noon, and the visitois had to remain under cover. /

After tea the Rev. Percy meson thanked all who had helped to maKe the trip a success, to those who had subscribed to the fund to get the conveyances, to those, who had lent ca:s, to Mr. A. H. Scholefield for the use of the hall, and to Miss White and Mr. Wright.

In seconding, kr. W. Twiss asked that their thanks be also given to Mr/. J. Peterson, who had kindly acted as marshal, to Mr. T. Dom- ville, who had given them kind advice, and to the ladies of the committee. Owing to various troubles arising out of the war they had been wondering whether to have the annual trip o. not. Responses, however, had been better than they expected, and they were deeply grateful to all who had helped in any way. (Applause.) The return journey was commenced about 6.30 p.m., and Warrington was safely reachNi about an hour later. The decrease in the num- ber of cripples this year as compared with last, when the number was 136, is accounted for by the facts that a few have died, others haiie entered employment, whilst others had tem- porary afflictions.

The reference to the Park Parliament in last week's " Gossip " suggests the observation that I have found an equally well-established deliberative assembly of greybeards and ancient wiseacres and' quidnuncs in the prin- cipal park of every town in which I have lived. TheSr carry the habit with them to the seaside, 4nd in the sheltered 'seats in front of the Metro- pole, Blackpool, you may find them in the season holding forth with all the customary fervour. At home it is their pleasant practice to monopolise a particular summer-house when in session, and to resent a stranger's intrusion diving a sitting. .When I was at Rochdale, the members' claim in this respect was frankly recognised by the Parks Committee, and they not only reserved the old men a shelter, but during the winter months heated it by means of a stove afid ventilated the roof so that they might smoke in comfort. The Orford soldier's account of his chat with a French woman recalled • what a young acquaintance of my own told me of somewhat similar experiences. div.head: CYCLING AND MOTORING.
div.p: CYCLING AND MOTORING.

SOME TIPS FIOR TOURISTS. Never forget in cycle touring that pleasure is measured by the hour, not by the mile. You miss half the pleasure if you are always worrying whether you can reach so and so by supper time. "Take it easy" should be your maxim for the first day at any rate. Too long a dars ride at the be- ginning of the tour will often spoil the whole holi- day. Start with a good breakfast, have a halt by the wayside and a refresher at eleven, a light lunch • at one, a light tea at four, and a good supwr at the end of the day's run. Rest half an hour after luncheon. Carry a few sticks of chocolate in the toolbag, not in your pocket. They will keep you going if no refreshment is handy. Soap your socks inside and out if there is any tender(cy to soreness of the feet on the road. Drink is bad when cycling. The more you drink the more thirsty you become. But you won't become thirsty if you ride with your mouth shut. Sleep in a village inn, not in a town hotel. That will cut down your expenses by half. It is quite easy to tour on ss. per day. So long as you keep riding, wet clothes need not worry you, but before you rest change at least your under- clothing. Don't try to " dust " each other or any other cyclists you may meet. Sudden speed bursts simply tire you and spoil the day's total. Remem- ber, too, that two's company and three isn't. If more than two go, let it be four or six, never three or five. Odd numbers are always an awkward rid- ing squad.

THE CYCLEMOTOR. A contemporary gives some interesting particu- lars of a new Canadian invention, known as the tyclemotor. It is a small motor attachment for an ordinary cycle of 1 h.P. rating, and the complete power plant—engine, magneto, carburettor, -.and exhaust box—fits into any ordinary frame, and attached to the seat pillar tube in two places. This appears to be a weakness, and it would seem that tome way of attaching it to the diagonal 'tube from the bottom of the head to the bottom bracket would be desirable. The point, however, is so obvious that it Can hardly be overlooked. The silencer box is attached directly to the cylinder and points for- ward, and the magneto is attached to the front of the base chamber. An ingenious method is em- ployed of making a single chain drive the magneto, and also convey the power of the engine to a coun- tershaft. The mileage per gallon is only estimated at 80 to 100, an astonishingly low figure, it seems to me. The weight of the complete plant is 211 b., of which the magneto is responsible for lflb. It is possible, therefore, to produce a very light machine with the aid of the " Cyclemotor," but it is doubt- ful whether the ordinary bicycle frame is suffi- ciently strong for use with it. The frame, of course, is quite able to carry an extra 211 b. weight, but the vibration set up by the engine would subject it to strains no ordinary frame ,would 'stand, Particu- larly as it is claimed the engine will revolve at 4,200 per minute.

A motor car is a wonderful piece of machinery, but it certainly falls far short of the ideal in one point, namely, the inability of the carburettor to do its work properly. The object of this instrument is to con- vert petrol into vapOur and to mix it with that amount of air which will cause an explosion ex- actly suited to the conditions under which the engine is working. The conditions vary frequently, and it is here that the modern carburettor fails. The so-called right mixture is a fallacy. Every change in condition requires a change in the mix- ture, i.e., if the full measure of comfort and. ease in 'driving are to be attained. THE PERFECT MIXTURE.

There is no such thing as a perfect mixture for general work. The ideal mixture would be one that gives the most effective explosion, whatever the conditions as regards road surface, individual practice, and atmosphere. What we really want is a carburettor which will work, not necessarily automatically, though, that means simplicity, but according to the special requirements of the moment. It does not always follow that one wants to fhange gear when negotiating a hill. When one is travelling slowly on high gear, the explosion speed should be slower awn would be absolutely correct for explosion efficiency. Flexibility really means the convenience of being able to climb hills without the noise and labour of changing gear. With the present day carburettor this is next to impossible. Who will be the first to give us the ideal? Whoever does, will not only be a benefactor to motorists, but will reap great financial rewards. SPOKE.

div.p: A TIPPLING SAILOR.
Falls From ,Express At Sankey And Is
Killed.

There fell from an express train rushing through Sankey Station on Thursday of last week a Southarapton sailor, who, whilst in a 'hotel at Derby had consumed five pints of beer. He was killed instantlyond at the inquest, held at the Chapel House Inn; Sankey, on Monday, it was stated that the deceased—Sidney Cooper, 21 years of age, a fireman in the employ of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, and resid- ing at 51, Empress-road; Southampton—left Southampton Docks Station for Liverpool on Thursday. along with a number of men, intend- ing to join a ship. They had with them a gallon of beer, which they drank in the train. On arriving at Derby they broke the journey, and Cooper and one of ,the company went to a hotel. Cooper had tie pints of beer, and the other men left him and his companion. At 9 p.m. the two latter• joined the train and travelled alone in a compartment, where they lay down and had a sleep. On arrival at War- rington. thp ticket-collector took the ticket of one of the men, but was unable to rouse Cooper. The other man again dozed off, and was awak- ened about ten minutes later by the carriage door banging. 'He then noticed that Cooper was missing. Hp pulled the communication cord, ,and upon a search being Made deceased was p found lying on his back in the six-foot way. He had sustained a fractured skull and ether injuries.
Verdict: "Accidental death." POLICE, RAILWAY OFFICIAL, AND JURYMAN AS BEARERS.

div.p: PRIVATE JACK LEIGH.
Dangerously 11l With Cholera.

News has this week been received to the effect that Private Jack 'Leigh, of the South Lancashire Regiment, is dangerously ill Ivith cholera. The news was conveyed through the medium of a telegram sent by the officer in command of records and received by his wife, which read as follows :—" I regret to inform you that a report has just been received to the effect that your husband, 11573 Private Jack Leigh, of the South .Trancashire .pegi- ment, is dangerously ill with cholera.---O.C. Records."

Private Jack _Leigh is a very well-known local lad, having lived in Lymm all his life. He was 32 Years old last Saturday, and judging by this report he must have spent his birth-2 day under very unpleasant circumstances. He joined the Army in August, 1914, and since then he has had some very trying experiences. div.head: CIDER AT MIDNIGHT.
div.p: CIDER AT MIDNIGHT.
Sergeants Climb Ladder And Look Through Bar Window.
LANDLADY AND GREEN-MAN HEAVILY FINED.

Just before midnight on the "Beautiful First of June," Sergeants Davies, and Griffiths heard voices in the bar of the Nag's Head, and, the lower part of the window being glazed, they procured a ladder and there saw the landlady, Mrs. Butterfield, Mrs. Jackson, and Xames Struthers, of Statham. The last-named was drinking some dark-coloured liquid from a glass. "Beer," thought the officers, and knocked at the door.

The story was 'told at the Petty Sessions on Wednesday, when Mrs. Butterfield was scharged with supplying intoxicating liquor to Struthers during prohibited' hours; and Struthers was charged with consuming it, and also with oeihe on licensed premises during closing hours. The case for the:polici.-was conducted by Mr. Caldecott,. of Knutsford, who said that when the policemen entered the Nag's Head Mrs. Butterfield pointed out the glass which Struthers had used., Sergeant Davies examined it and observed that it_smelt as if beer had just been in it, but Mrs. Butterfield said, "No, it's, not beer. It is cider." Mr. Caldecott pointed out to their Worships that even if the liquid were cider ilind not beer that 'also was against the law, because cider was classified as an ih- toxicating drink, and a licence had to be obtained to sell the same; in fact, cider was twice as strong as small beer. The Mrs. Jack- son present was employed at the Nag's Head, mainly helping in the catering department. The Sergeants gave evidence and then Mr. Arthur Browne, of Warrington, who defended, said that Mrs. Butterfield did not know cider was intoxicating. As for Struthers being on the premises during prohibited hours, he was entitled -to be there,. although a threshing mac.thine proprietoridie worked on the bowling green at nights, and did mostof the heavy work about the inn. He also had a bedroom there which lie occupied not infrequently. ~. Mrs. Butterfield and' Struthers gave evidence confirming their solicitor's statement, Struthers remarking, in addition, that when he was drinking the cider he thought he was drinking minerals.

The magistrates were in retirement consider- ing their judgment for about twenty, minutes, and upon their returning the Chairman (Vi.;e- Chancellor Stewart Smith, K.C.), said they were going to find Struthers guilty of consuming in toxicating liquor during prohibited hours, and would take no notice of the other charge against him as the police did not press the mattcr. "We have heard the evidence in this case," added the Chairman; "but we are by no means satisfied that we have heard the whole truth. Mrs. Butterfield will be fined £lO •and also ordered to pay £2 2s. advocate's fee, to :r.e solicitor for the prosecution, and Struthers will be fined £5 and will have to pay £1 is. ad %to- eate's fee."

Cou-ncillor W. G. Groves, in objecting, stated that business men who came for exemption in nine cases out of ten, could not find time to attend drills.—Councillor IL A. Gotobed was surprised at such a remark from an old Volun- teer, and having done so much service.—The Chairman remarked that he agreed with both menibers. A master builder, in making appeals for six employes, stated that Ifour of the men appealed for were making ammunition boxes for the Government, and the other two were engaged doing repairs at tanyards where war material was being. produced. He had made an applica- tion to get these ammunition box makers badged, and yesterday had a visit from a Board of 'Trade official, and he himself stilted that three out of four could not be spared. I He had 40 men at present.—Could not some of these 'men be put on the tannery work ?--At great inconvenience; some are on at present.— The military repres,entative stated that the military authorities' view of these cases was that *if these men were granted exemption the Army would be none the richer. They had got skilled in these machines in a very short time, ;and others could do the same.—The Tribunal decided, to adjourn the four cases of men 'employed on ammunition boxes pending the Board of Trade official's report. Farmer and Butcher's Successful Appeal.

A man who carried on business as a farmer and butcher stated that he had serious business obligations, He had been in business 17 years, and if, called to the Colours he would have to close down. Mr. G. L. Welford (solicitor), who represented applicant, stated that the man had a widowed mother and invalid sister depending on him. He had to look after a farm of 11 acres, and a butcher's shop 'which demanded a rental of 216 a year and 'rates.—Has he a brother?—Yes.—Could not he look after the businese—No.-tMr. Welford added that this

business was engaged in the production of food, and it was an absolute necessity that it should be carried on. It was a considerable business, and its closing down would mean a loss to Lymm. Four acres of the farm land were arable and in addition there were three acres of fruit and vegetables. •He had no one assisting who could take charge. He had one sister assisting in the shop, but she'could not possibly 'manage the business. At the outbreak of war he had three men working for him, but they had left him. He could not say whether they were in the Army or not.—Have you any men assisting you at present F—Yes. One young man who is unfit for the Army, and a youth of sixteen, but Ihe could not leave the business in their hands. —Absolute exemption was granted. Builders Seek Exemption For Eight Men.

In appealing for eight men, one of them the principal partner, a firm of builders stated that they had a lot of work in hand, including 18 new cottages, which were being built for agri- cultural purposes. The material for these cot- tages had all been bought, and if they were not allowed to keep their men Until they were, com- pleted they would suffer serious financial loss.— When did you make these contracts ?—February. 1916.—Cannot you-arrange for the painting and plumbing to be done through other sources ? We do not see that .we could.—Would not some other trader make some arrangement for rou?— They will have enough to do to look after their own. We have applied for labour at four different Labour Bureaux, but been unsuccessful. —How many men did you employ at the out- break of war ?-62.—How many of these have enlisted ?—Nineteen. The last one went last Thursday.—How long have, these men now appealed for been in your employ ?—From five to 25 years.—Have you taken any steps to see how the people would treat you if your contracts had to be broken ?—No.—Applicants further stated that out of 25 eligible men working for them, 19 had gone to the Colours, 17 of whom were voluntary enlistments. If the remaining men had to go it would mean stopping about double their number of old men.—Conditional exemption was granted to the chief partner, and of .the others, five were granted exemption until October Ist, and the other two until July 16th. Tradesman Appeals for Carter.

A tradesman, in appealing for his carter, stated that owing to the shortage in labour he had great difficulty in getting his goods in and out. He had a big country trade, and it meant a man being out all day. The man appealed for, independent of his carting, had the horses and 12 pigs to look after.—How many men have you? —Just the one.—Have you any assistants in the Shop 2—Only the family.—How many children have you ?—Two bays and one girl.—What age are'they P—The eldest boy,is 18, the girl 16, and the younger boy 14.—What does the eldest boy do P—He is on munitions.—How long has ne been on munitions?—Quite twelve months.--Is he badged ?—Yes.—What does your youngest boy do P—He is a clerk.—Have you the same number of men now as you had .before the war? —Yes.—Then the war has not yet affected you? —No.—Temporary exemption till August Ist. Off-licence ,Holder's Liabilities.

A grocer, provision dealer and off-licence )iolder, in appealing for exemption on personal grounds, stated that he took over the business after his mother's death, and had to look after the business under his mother's will until his youngest brother was 21 years of 'age. This brother at present is only 19.—D0 you do any- thing else 'besides look after the business?—No, practically nothing.—What do you mean hy practically nothing?—Well, I do a few odd jobs fitting electric bells, &c.—Could not your wife. manage the buginess in your absence P—l sup- pose she could, but it would be with great diffi- culty.—Have you ever had anyone to help you ? I have had girls, but they do not feel inclined to stop.—Temporary exemption till July 16th.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS.— Colonel Arthur Stanleigh and Judge Lamar Stan- leigh, cousins, of Virginia, are bitter enemies over the possession of The Diamond from the Sliy, a rnasaive jewel heirloom found centuries ago in. a fallen meteor. Colonel Stanleigh when a daughter Is born buys the male heir of a gipsy 'king, that he may keep the jewel. He plans to rear Esther, the girl, in secrecy. Esther and The Diamond from the Sky are stolen by Hagar, the gipsy mother. Years later Hagar returns Esther and the diamond, but of the old group only Dr. Lee is living. Blair Stanleigh kills Dr. Lee and steals the jewel. Then Blair Stanleigh and Arthur Stan- 'bleb, the false heir, fight a duel. Arthur, thinking he has killed his cousin, flees in a racing motor car. In his mag., flight the,machine goes over a river bank, and that nit the moon shines on a body floating down the stream. On the breast of the man gleams The Diamond from the Sky.

div.head: CHAPTER IV.
div.p: CHAPTER IV.

3 THE PRODIGAL'S PROGRESS. Such buoyant spirits as Esther'e could not easily 14,6 quenched. She had grown to by, the old ,doctor, but now he was dead it was delightful to be back again with the woman she regarded as Mother.

In —The early dawn the girl went down to the stream for water, and there, lying by the side, was the body of a'man. "Arthur," cried the girl, "speak to sue. Oh, Arthur, do speak. What are you doing here?" " Mother ! mother!" pealed a voice through the quiet of the camp. "Coma quickly, Arthur is here --dead!" Hearing Esther's call of distress, Viagar sped to the banks of the stream. Before the startled gipsies followed Hagar discovered that her son was alive. She found, too, that he was wearing The Diamond from the Sky. Distracting Esther's attention she quietly unclasped the jewel and hid it. Then the unconscious form was tenderly borne to Hagar's luxurious van. As he was slowly struggling back to life the Bh.eriff of .Fairfax County•dame to the camp. I am looking for e man named Arthur Stan- he said to Hagar. "He has,killed Dr. Lee, the old doctor of Fairfax, and will be hanged for it."

"I have not seen him," lied Hagar, "but if you wi,s,h You may search the camp." A waste of time. The gay Arthur Stanleigh ""'4lcl not hide amongst such a crowd as this, aneered the sheriff. Was with blazing eyes that Hagar confronted Alt Was when he was strong enough to bear hez erce reproaches. "My sacrifice has been all in vain,'* she cried, bitterly. "A ruined man and a Murderer, you have wasted every chance in your life for which I bowed my head in bitterness and sorrow. Better had you been bred the poor giPeY You were born rather than to be the fugitive im- poster who has squandered a heritage that was not his." Arthur regarded her as though she were what she seerded to him, an insane harridan, who raged at him in half-coherent frenzy. "Who are you?" he asked, amazed. "Who am I? Well might you ask. You, who boastfully imagine that you are Arthur Stanleigh of Stanleigh Hall. Bah! I am your mother!" " What? Am I a eipsy?"

" Yes, a gipsy; a real gipsy, with an untainted ancestry. Better be a good gipsy than -a fugitive Murderer. Look here "—drawing a brass-bound box from its hiding-place and handing him a sealed document, yellow with age—" read that."

On the 'outside were the words: "To be opened only after my death, in case my son, Arthur Stan- leigh, should prbve unworthy of the name of Stan- leigh." With tremblina hands he broke the seal and learned the dreadful truth.
"Nothing belongs to you, not even your name, and much less this for which you stained your hands in blood," cried Hagar, throwing down with a. Feature of disdain The Diamond from the Sky.

But," said he, "I am riot guilty of the death of Dr. Lee; he was my friend. I did kill my sup- 1/cseirl cousin, Blair, and he now lies in a grave dug for another, bat not for this," and he pointed to the jewel. I killed Blair Stanleigh because he spoke ill of Esther. Tell me. if I am not Arthur Stanleigh, who is she? Is she my sister? I ask this, for by every wild deed of my reckless life in the past and for every good I hope to achieve, I love her." " No matter who she is, you are not good enough to breathe the same air with her," replied Hagar, fiercely. " Make a name for yourself in the place of the one you have lost, then return to me for a Mother's blessing." So saying, Hagar left the young man to his own thoughts in the van and walked away. Arthur had !eel' his mother place the diamond in the box, and ~.11 her agitation she had left the van without it. he was not Arthur Stanleir,h he was not heir to 'fle diamond, but he was determined that Blair Stanleigh's mother should not have the jewel, which Would be Blair's if he had lived. Bagar was almost frantio with rage when she discovered that Arthur had taken the precious dia- Mond& She determined that Esther, deprived of erY birthright, should have the jewel; and with is object in view engaged the services of Tom -ulake, an astute detective, to trace Arthur, and, if Possible, find out the truth concerning the death °f Dr. Lee, whom she did not believe had been killed by Arthur. No suspicion had been directed at Blair in con- with the doctor's murder, and when the i;tle and cry after Arthur was hottest Blair accepted 'ija mother's suggestion and went to Richmond. It therefore came about that both the young men were iI the town at the same time, but while Arthur hid himself in humble lodgings, Blair " lorded " it with 916 best at a swagger hotel. Blair was endeavour- to forget his peril, present and prospective, in "Id and reckless indulgences. Every night he larabled at the exclusive establishment of Abe I°°ro. Finding himself cleaned out at this urxurious temple of chance; he induced the clever Mr. Bloom to cash a cheque for two thousand dollars on the Bank of Fairfax, knowing full well that it would be returned marked "No funds." At that risk Blair smiled; he would recoup himself fat the tables and laugh in the man's face when the "rlith was known. But the five thousand went the M1,,,—,15-f-Wee7teeeeeeeeeecort)fr \.O
waY of the other dollars. and Blair was reduced to the extremity of pawning his watch to try again the Goddess of Fortune.

"Down on his uppers," Arthur resolved to raise money on the diamond. and Ike Bloom, brother and partner of Abe Bloom, readily advanced the three hundred dollars the young man asked for the wonderful jewel. As he turned to leave he heard a voice say, " want fifty dollars on this watch." He staggered, lalf-fainting with fear and joy, against the parti- tion, It was the voice of Blair Stanleigh. There could be no mistake. In a revulsion of feeling to find that he was not a murderer, Arthur waited until Blair came out, and with a cry of delight greeted him. Surprised, and feigning joy, Blair expressed his satisfaction at seeing his cousin. Then he made haste to explain that Dr. Lee had called him to his study and had given him the diamond. The old man, who was greatly agitated, fell dead across his study table. "I was afraid I should be suspected of killing him for the diamond. How could I explain when you gave me no opriortunity?" asked Blair, lying glibly. "I was .roo frightened to explain, and you were too angry to listen to me. The wound was only a slight one. But a detective has been put upon the track, and if he finds a clue your evidence would only serve to implicate me, and I am innocent." _

Thinking. that Dr. Lee had at last repented the deed of years ago, Arthur believed the story told him. So for the time being he resolved to keep Hagar's secret—and his own. In the foolish, impulsive generosity of his nature, Arthur promised to stand by Blair. Heaving a sigh of relief the young man who had done the old doctor to death said. "You do not know my mother's cousin, Mrs. Buxton Randolph, who gives the grand ball in Richmond to-night. Come, let us have one good fling; one good time together, in memory of the days at Stanleigh Hall. If you go in your assumed name of 'John Powell' you will be safe. There is a stunning young New York widow—lots of money and style about her—l want you to meet. I want your approval of her." To Richmond on the night of the ball came Hagar, bringing with her Esther, and, as half servant, half bodyguard, her gipsy lieutenant, Luke Lovell. By appointment Hagar met Tom Blake and learned that not only was Arthur in Richmond, but also Blair, and they were going to the ball. On many occasions Hagar had turned such functions as this to good account, and with Esther she deter- mined to appear as a fortune teller, confront Arthur, and get the diamond before he left the town. Best of all was the news from Blake that he had thumb prints, which proved that Blair and not Arthur was guilty of the death of the doctor. The rich young New York " widow " with whom Blair was infatuated was Vivian Marston, a gay New Yorker, but certainly not known to the best class of people in the great city. She had met Mrs. Randolph at Palm Beech the previous winter, and had been invited to Richmond. Vivian desired to create a stir at the ball, and having no jewels re- membered her old friend, Abe Bloom, who received the supposed New York society leader with an astonishing air of familiarity. "Abe, old dear," the fair vision said, "I am going to that big blow-out to-night. I want to pick up some rich guy of Richmond and marry and settle down among the southern aristocracy. I have plenty of fine clothes, but no jewels. I want you to fix me out."

" give you a note to brother Ike," said Abe, and the lady departed from Mr. Bloom's establish- ment with a compelling note to his brother, the pawnbroker. The best Ike had in the shop was The Diamond from the Sky. In a fatal moment he displayed it to the opulent-looking lady friend of his brother, and that dazzled young lady had eyes for none of the other treasures. "Be careful of it," warned the cautious Bloom. "You will be wearing one of the finest diamonds in the world."

"It can't be too good for me, Mr. Bloom," said Vivian, as she gazed enraptured at the great jewel in its antique setting. That night Vivian Marston, in all her luxuriant beauty, set off as it was by the diamond blazing on her fair bosom, was the cynosure of all eyes at Mrs. Randolph's ball as she stood with her host receiving the guests. Arthur and Blair gasped at her beauty, but stared as if turned to stone to see The Diamond from the Sky gleaming on the bosom of this stranger to Richmond. How came it there? was the thought of both of them. For in all their reconciliation they had sedulously avoided discussing the baleful gem. Others besides wondered what it meant. Hagar saw the jewel sparkling, and called the detective's attention to the extraordinary occur- rence. "There is a deep mystery here," said Hagar to Blake.

Outside Luke loitered idly, waiting to guard Esther and Hagar back from the ball. "Shall we have the fortunes first?" asked the hostess of Vivian Marston. "It will be great fun and help to get things started." Hagar had given no sign of recognition to Arthur, and he in turn was relieved that his gipsy mother did not seem intent on creating any scene. He stood aloof with Blair, and was silent. Both of them gazed from afar, as though fascinated by the ' diamond blazing on the breast of the strange guest. How had she come into possession of the Stanleigh • "charm against harm" ? "I have a Wondrous fortune to tell this lady." said Hagar, huskily, as she indicated Vivian. "Will the lady go aside and wait for me?" "What fun! You must tell me all your wondrous • fortune. Now, don't forzet," exclaimed Mrs. Ran- ' dolph as Vivian Marston smiled and nodded assent to this. She glided away to a seat by a low, heavily-curtained window in the small room adjoin- ing the ballroom. Vivian had just seated herself with the serene satisfaction that she was the sensation of the evening—she and the great blazing gem upon her breast. Then she saw Hagar, leaving Esther to be •gently patronised'by Mrs. Randolph, coming in her direction. She settled herself back in the low gilt chair against the velvet hangings of the window, and then she felt a strong hand clutch at her throat, throttling her through the curtains so that she could not shriek aloud. Then a brawny fore- arm drew back her shapely neck, and the strangling hand loosened its hold and snatched away The Diamond from the Sky, (To be continued.) ,tf,t' • Detnce, • eceereemi

div.head: SOLDIER'S POMERANIAN.
div.p: SOLDIER'S POMERANIAN.
Rites Children Playing In The Street.

The story pf a dog which has bitten the same boy three times in eight months, was told at the Borough Police Co,urt on Thursday, 'viler. Thomas Foy, 56, Cockhedge-lane, was charged with keeping a ferocious dog which was not under control.

The complainant, Mrs. tflvlin, of 54, Cock- hedge-lane, said her boy was bitten OR the right kg one day recently, and sh,. thought the 41.4 should he .kept Jinder proper control. Margaret Mannion; Cockhedge-lane, said the same dog bit her daughter five months ago. Every child in the street was terrified of .it. Mr. C. H. Unsworth, for the defendant, said the boy and two others were playing hi the street, and when struggling for a ball the dog ran amongst them, evidently thinking they were fighting. The dog was only a small pomeranian, and was most playful. It would make friends with anybody. The dog was not Mr. Foy's property, but his son's, who was fighting at the Front, and he was anxious that it should be kept until he returned. Mr. Foy was very sorry for what had happened. In imposing a fine of 10s. the Chairman of the Ben& (Mr. J. Rymer Young) said the dog must be kept under control.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKING MEN'S ASSOCIATION.
N.A. CENTRE.
A GOOD OPENING.

All members, with few exceptions, were off last week-end to try their favourite waters. Some were , after the weighers, others were getting their hand in for the coming contests. Very few returned with- out being fairly well satisfied with the opening. The Weaver, Norton. Chester. Aintree, and Chirk were well represented, the Weaver about taking the honours for the best catch; and the Shropshire Union Canal for the best: specimen. •

div.head: Norton.
div.p: Norton.

The roach in this water appeared in fine buckle. About fourteen were taken on Saturday, twenty on Monday, and eighteen on Tuesday. The best indi- vidual catch fell to R. Dunbobbin on the Monday, when he took a dozen nice sizable roach. The Weaver.

At Northwich end on the Weaver the best were Messrs. Hewitt and Jolley. A catch of ten or eleven pounds of fish in one and a half days is not so bad from here, while bream 111 b. and perch up to 1(k)z. were taken. A couple of dace were also caught just below the sluices.

div.head: Chester.
div.p: Chester.
The canal here yielded the best sport. Catches of roach ranged from four to eight oz., one member having fourteen roach. Eels and flounders were the most numerous fish caught in the Dee. '

div.head: Aintree.
div.p: Aintree.

The Leeds and Liverpool Canal was tried by four members, more for testing its merits as a contest water than anything else. As regards practice for contest fishing, this canal can satisfy almost any angler. It must be teeming with gudgeon, as no sooner had you got your bait settled on the bottom than the float began to dip, and you could catch gudgeon almost every other sail down. If it is in the same order on Sunday for the contest, speed will play an important part, but if the roach are moving the novice generally turns up best •here. Two seasons ago in four contests there were four different winners, and if my memory serves me right there was not anyone in the first three on two consecutive occasions.

div.head: Chirk and District.
div.p: Chirk and District.

The Sbiopahire Union Canal around here is fish- ing fire. The canal is visited by our members who are at Park Hall Camp, Oswestry, Mr. H. Moore playing the leading part as usual. Catches of roach are reported, and everyone a handful, say, from eight to fourteen oz. We hear that on Tues- day one was safely landed by H. Moore 11b. 2oz. This sort of roach should be recorded on the set board by all means, as a 11b. roach is not caught every day.

In this, the second' year of the war, when we are keen on curtailing kill, unnecessary dxpendi- ture, we in Warringion and district should be especially grateful tuat the Royal Show, which opens on Tuesday, is to ;Je held almost at our doors. It coveis 110 acres. in the Withington district of Manehester, a penny tramcar or train journey from the city taking one to the venue. By some it .has been questioned whether the holding'of a show this year was the right thing, but the promoters have no doubt on that score. As Sir Daniel McCabe Aremarked at the Press luncheon given by the honorary director, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., at the Midland Hotel, on Monday, agriculture is the 'largest industry in the country, and should receive every encouragement possible. To-day we depend upon our live stock, its development and multiplying, and upon our fields and 'gardens more than at any other time in recent history. The more we can improve the breed of cattle, and the more we can tickle the 'earth and make it smile into fertility the better. There are no finer breeders of 4 cattle in the world than in England. Therefore, Sir Daniel contended, it is most important for us to attend carefully to agriculture; ail(' it would have been a mistake not to have held the show this year. That is ,an opinion generally endorsed; eloquently endorsed especially by the number of entries received. The live stock side of the exhibition is to be on the usual comprehensive scale as regards classification and prizes, and the total, entries are more numerous than at Not- tingham.' last year.' The show will combine almost all the features of "the Royal" in peace times.

'PREVENTING CLOVER BLOAT IN CATTLE. When first turning cattle on clover it should be done gradually until the digestive organs become accustomed to the change. The safest way is not to permit them to eat fresh clover 4...•,r longer than 20 minutes or half an hour the first

day, and .increase the time of feeding each day Until the full grazing time is reached. It is not safe tolturn cattle on fresh green pasture until the dew or frost is gone. Another method is to give the cattle some dry feed, such as hay, be- fore turning them on clover. This tends to pre- vent fermentation of the green feed, and when the stomach of the animal has accommodated itself to the change from dry to green food the animal may consume large quantities of green food without bad results. We are no* conduct- ing studies which. will determine ,the value of various substances as preventives of clover bloat, and hope to have, in the near future, some valuable information. For acute bloating we strongly recommend drenching' the animal with 1 quart of a 1+ per cent. solution of formalin, followed by placing a wooden block in the animal's mouth, and gentle exercise if the animal can get up. Formalin is a trade name for a 40 per cent. solution of formaldehyde gas in water and may be obtained at any chemist's. Half an ounce of formalin in 1 quart of water makes the proper solution with which to drench the animal. When an animal has once bloated, great care should be used to avoid a second bloating, as such animals are often peculiarly liable to bloat again. We have now used this treatment for three years and so far have n.)t lost a single case.—" Breeders' Gazette."

Whatever profit roily be derived from feeding cake or meal to cows when they are in full milk shortly after calving, it is very questionable if it pays under ordinary conditions to try to ex- tend the milking period by the liberal 'use f cake and meal when cows are beginning to go dry. A mistake is frequently made in continu- ing to draw cows (it can scarcely be called milking) when they are almost dry, and thereby reducing their condition. In, these circum- stances, says "Farm and Home," it is more profitable to put the rows dry altogether and allow them a moderato rest, so that they may comMence the succeeding laetation period under the most favourable conditions. No hard and fast rule can be laid down as'regards either the kind or quality of food to use. So much rle- pends on the home-grown produce at the farmer's disposal, the relative market price of the different feeding stuffs, the yield of earth individual ,cow and the price realised for the produce.
